display.title: Simchas Beis Hashoeva Night 3: The Alter Rebbe and the Rich Man's Nickel
display.summary_short: At a live Sukkos rally, children say the Twelve Pesukim and hear how the Alter Rebbe freed an orphan groom by accepting a rich man's single nickel with a smile.
display.summary_long: Recorded live at a Simchas Beis Hashoeva rally for children during Sukkos 5786. Rabbi Goldstein welcomes the crowd and jokes with Simcha Engel about the new year, then groups of children come up to recite the Twelve Pesukim, and everyone says and sings Al Tira together. Rabbi Goldstein explains that tonight's Ushpizin, Yaakov Avinu and the Alter Rebbe, both excelled in learning Torah, and tells a story of the Alter Rebbe. The Alter Rebbe arrives for the wedding of two orphans whose match he had made, only to find that the town official has seized the groom to send him to the Russian army for twenty-five years. The official demands 1,500 rubles, and the poor town cannot raise even half. With Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev and Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Horodok, the Alter Rebbe visits the richest man in town, known for giving only a nickel. He accepts the nickel with a smile and a warm brachah, and the man keeps calling them back with more, until he breaks down, tells why he had stopped giving tzedakah, and pays the whole ransom. The wedding goes ahead with great joy, and the evening ends with a lesson about reaching every Jew's heart.
display.lesson: Every Jew is good at heart. Speak to him gently, with a smile and a brachah, show him how much you love him, and he will give with an open heart.

date.note: Year 5786 said on air; 'tonight the Ushpizin are Yaakov Avinu and the Alter Rebbe' = third night of Sukkos (Wednesday evening, 8 Oct 2025).

advisories.note: A hostile official seizes a Jewish groom on his wedding day to draft him into the army for 25 years; he is ransomed.
The cruel official later falls from his horse and dies; told briefly.

characters: the poor man who refused the nickel

sources_cited.note: The Rebbe's call to say the Twelve Pesukim whenever children gather (as cited).
